topics.title: Irony in 'A Question of Trust': proverbs

learn.hook: A master thief who plans everything perfectly is fooled in five minutes by a charming stranger!
points: 'A Question of Trust' by Victor Canning is about Horace Danby, a respected lock-maker who secretly robs one safe a year to buy rare books.
While robbing a house, he meets a young woman who pretends to be the lady of the house. She persuades him to open the safe for her and leaves with the jewels.
Horace had taken off his gloves, so his fingerprints are on the safe. He is arrested for a theft he was tricked into, and nobody believes his story.
The irony: a clever thief is himself cheated by another thief; the careful planner who left nothing to chance ends up trusting the wrong person.
Proverbs sum up such lessons: 'As you sow, so shall you reap' means we face the results of our own actions.

example.q: Passage: Mr Bose, who sells 'unbreakable' anti-theft locks in Kolkata, returned from his shop one evening to find that his own scooter had been stolen from outside his house. Why is this situation ironic?
steps: Mr Bose sells locks that are supposed to stop theft.
Yet his own scooter is stolen.
The outcome is the opposite of what we would expect for him, so it is situational irony.
example.answer: It is situational irony: a seller of anti-theft locks becomes a victim of theft himself.

learn.reallife: News sometimes reports ironic events, like a 'No Parking' board being towed away, and readers enjoy the twist.

games.title: Proverb and meaning
pairs: As you sow, so shall you reap.
you face the results of your actions
All that glitters is not gold.

games.title: Story and irony check
items: Horace Danby steals to buy rare books.
He robs one safe a year to buy rare books.
The young woman is really the owner of the house.
She is a thief pretending to be the lady of the house.
Horace is caught because of his fingerprints.
He removed his gloves before opening the safe.
The story's irony is that a thief is tricked by another thief.
'A Question of Trust' was written by Ruskin Bond.
It was written by Victor Canning.

quiz.q: Why does Horace Danby steal in 'A Question of Trust'?
options: To buy rare and expensive books
To pay off a big debt
quiz.explain: He robs one safe a year and spends the money on rare books.
quiz.mistake: Gives a common motive not in the story

quiz.q: What is Horace Danby's regular job?
quiz.explain: He is a respected locksmith, which helps him open safes.

quiz.q: Who tricks Horace into opening the safe?
options: The real owner of the house
A young woman pretending to be the lady of the house
quiz.explain: She pretends the house is hers and asks him to open the safe.

options: His fingerprints are found on the safe
quiz.explain: He had taken off his gloves, so his fingerprints were on the safe.
quiz.mistake: Invents a different way he was caught

quiz.q: What is the main irony in 'A Question of Trust'?
options: A clever thief is himself cheated by another thief
The jewels were made of chocolate
quiz.explain: Horace, who fooled everyone, is fooled by the woman.
quiz.mistake: Misses the twist of the cheater being cheated

quiz.q: Passage: Mr Bose, who sells 'unbreakable' anti-theft locks in Kolkata, returned from his shop one evening to find that his own scooter had been stolen from outside his house. What type of irony is this?
quiz.explain: A lock seller being robbed is the opposite of what we expect.

quiz.q: What does 'As you sow, so shall you reap' mean?
options: Work hard and you will be rich
You face the results of your own actions
quiz.explain: The proverb uses farming to say actions bring matching results.

quiz.q: Which proverb best fits Horace's fate?
options: Early to bed, early to rise.
A stitch in time saves nine.
As you sow, so shall you reap.
quiz.explain: Horace's dishonest actions bring him punishment.
quiz.mistake: Picks a well-known proverb that does not match the story

teach.ask: Gappu: A thief got tricked by another thief? Is that irony? And what does 'as you sow, so shall you reap' mean?
teach.praise: Chirp! The cheater got cheated: irony! And we reap the results of what we do. Lesson learnt!
teach.nudge: Who got fooled in the story, and why is that unexpected? What does the proverb say about actions?

topics.title: Crime words and reporting a crime

learn.hook: Burglar, alibi, accomplice: every detective and reporter needs these words!
points: Crime vocabulary: theft (stealing), burglary (breaking into a building to steal), forgery (making fakes), accomplice (helper in a crime), suspect (person thought guilty), alibi (proof you were elsewhere), witness (person who saw it).
A news report starts with a short headline and a dateline (place and date).
The first paragraph (the lead) answers the 5Ws and 1H: who, what, when, where, why, how.
News reports are factual and use the third person; the passive voice is common ('was arrested').
Crime stories in literature often end with justice, reminding readers that wrongdoing has consequences.

example.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Find who, what, when and where.
steps: Where: a bungalow in Koregaon Park, Pune.
example.answer: Who: a locksmith; what: arrested over missing jewellery; when: Tuesday; where: Koregaon Park, Pune.

learn.reallife: Newspapers like those you see at home follow this format every day: headline, dateline, then the key facts first.

items.text: The ___ told the police she saw a man jump the wall.
He had a strong ___: he was at a wedding in Nagpur that night.
The thief's ___ waited outside in the getaway car.
Police found ___ on the glass of the window.

options: Breaking into a building to steal
quiz.explain: Burglary is entering a building illegally to steal.
quiz.mistake: Confuses burglary with forgery or fraud

options: A person who helps someone commit a crime
A person who saw the crime
quiz.explain: An accomplice is a partner in a crime.

options: Proof that someone was elsewhere when a crime happened
quiz.explain: An alibi shows a suspect could not have done it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a piece of evidence against someone

options: A person who has been proven innocent
A person thought to have committed a crime
quiz.explain: A suspect is believed, but not yet proven, to be guilty.

quiz.q: What should the first paragraph of a news report answer?
options: Who, what, when, where, why and how
quiz.explain: The lead gives the key facts (5Ws and 1H).
quiz.mistake: Thinks a news report starts with background or opinion

quiz.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Where was the safe?
options: In a bungalow in Koregaon Park
quiz.explain: The report says 'a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow'.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a usual place for a safe

quiz.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Why does the report say 'was arrested' instead of naming who arrested him?
options: The reporter forgot the word police
The passive voice keeps the focus on the person arrested
It is in the future tense
quiz.explain: News reports often use the passive to focus on what happened to someone.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the passive with focus
Picks a word related to crime instead of its opposite

teach.ask: Gappu: I want to write a news report about the stolen worms in our garden! How do I start?
teach.praise: Breaking news, chirp! Headline, dateline, and the 5Ws first. Gappu reporting live!
teach.nudge: What goes at the top of a news report? Which questions should the first paragraph answer?
